summary.text: Temperature is a measure of how hot or cold something is, reflecting the average kinetic energy of the particles inside it.
It is read with a thermometer on scales such as Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin, each of which fixes a zero point and a size for one degree.
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest point on the scale, which experiments can approach very closely but never reach.

facts.label: Celsius anchors
facts.value: 0 °C is water freezing, 100 °C is water boiling

facts.label: Fahrenheit anchors
facts.value: Water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F

facts.label: Coldest reached
facts.value: About 38 trillionths of a kelvin in experiments

facts.label: Kelvin's status
facts.value: One of the seven SI base units

items.prompt: A kitchen warms by 5 °C over the afternoon. By how many kelvin did it warm?

options.label: 5 K

items.explain: A one degree Celsius step is the same size as a one kelvin step; the scales differ only by a fixed offset of 273.15.

items.prompt: A glass thermometer filled with mercury is pushed into a furnace far hotter than any kitchen oven. Why does it stop being useful?

options.label: The mercury turns to vapor, so the column no longer measures
Mercury stops expanding once it gets very hot
The glass shrinks faster than the mercury grows
Mercury contracts as it warms past a certain point

items.explain: Mercury-in-glass thermometers work only in a limited span; above mercury's boiling point they are impracticable.

items.prompt: Two identical cups hold water, and one cup is hotter. What differs between them at the microscopic level?

options.label: Its molecules are heavier than the others
It holds a larger number of molecules
Its molecules are packed in more tightly
Its molecules move with more energy on average

items.explain: Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy of the particles, so hotter water has faster-moving molecules.

items.prompt: Physicists keep cooling a sample in a lab, getting closer to absolute zero each time. What will they find?

options.label: They will reach it once the equipment is good enough
They can get extremely close but never actually arrive
Cooling becomes impossible below about one kelvin
They arrive, then the particles start speeding up again

items.explain: Absolute zero can be approached very closely but not reached, as the third law of thermodynamics recognizes.

items.prompt: A physicist wants a scale whose zero means the lowest temperature possible. Which scale fits?

options.label: Kelvin, because its zero sits at absolute zero
Celsius, because its zero is where water freezes
Fahrenheit, because 0 °F is the coldest ever measured
Any of them, since zero is arbitrary on every scale

items.explain: The Kelvin scale's numerical zero is absolute zero, which is why it is used predominantly for scientific purposes.

items.prompt: A designer thinks about filling a thermometer with water. Why could it mislead over certain stretches of temperature?

options.label: It expands far too much to fit in a thin tube
It evaporates completely at every temperature
It has no fixed freezing point to calibrate against
It shrinks as it warms in some stretches

items.explain: Most materials expand when warmed, but water contracts over some range, so it is hardly useful as a thermometric material there.
